summary: We developed PixFire, an interactive web platform that harmonizes historical satellite fire detection data from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors to enable more accurate comparisons and reliable wildfire analysis. The project addresses a major challenge in satellite monitoring: differences in spatial resolution between sensors. MODIS has an approximate spatial resolution of 1 km, while VIIRS operates at 375 m, causing artificial increases in detected fire activity when their records are directly combined.PIXFire processes 24 years of official NASA FIRMS data (2003–2026) through a reproducible Python pipeline, statistical calibration, and spatial aggregation, transforming inconsistent observations into a comparable historical dataset. Additionally, it incorporates statistical models and Monte Carlo simulations to analyze fire patterns and generate potential projections for 2027–2030.Currently focused on Bolivia, the platform allows users to explore historical fire activity, visualize geographic patterns, compare unharmonized and harmonized data, and examine future projections. Its validation results demonstrate errors within a ±15% threshold.PIXFire aims to support environmental authorities, agricultural communities, and emergency organizations by providing reliable information for wildfire monitoring and prevention. Its long-term vision is global expansion, helping protect human lives, agricultural activities, and ecosystems.
details:
What exactly does it do?

PIXFire is an interactive web platform designed to harmonize satellite fire detection data obtained from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors. Its main purpose is to reduce inconsistencies caused by differences in sensor spatial resolution and provide more reliable historical wildfire analysis.

Specifically, PIXFire:

  • Harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS sensor observations to make fire detection data comparable.
  • Processes 24 years of historical NASA FIRMS data (2003–2026), currently focused on Bolivia.
  • Identifies geographic and temporal patterns of wildfire activity.
  • Compares original, unharmonized data with corrected and harmonized data.
  • Integrates protected areas to examine the relationship between fire activity and conservation zones.
  • Uses statistical models and Monte Carlo simulations to generate potential wildfire projections for 2027–2030.
  • Provides interactive visualizations to support environmental analysis and decision-making.

How does it work?

The platform follows a structured data processing and analysis workflow:

  • Satellite Data Collection: Historical fire detection records are obtained from NASA FIRMS, using observations from the MODIS sensor aboard the Aqua satellite and the VIIRS sensor aboard the Suomi-NPP satellite.
  • Data Filtering and Processing: Satellite observations are filtered according to quality criteria and matching orbital pass times to improve consistency between sensors.
  • Spatial Harmonization: The observations are aggregated into spatial grids at three resolutions: 0.25°, 0.10°, and 0.05°. This process transforms inconsistent detections into comparable monthly measurements.
  • Statistical Calibration: Historical data are calibrated using seasonal patterns to reduce systematic differences between sensors and produce a consistent time series.
  • Fire Pattern Analysis: The platform analyzes historical trends, seasonal behavior, geographic distributions, and areas with the highest fire activity.
  • Predictive Modeling: Statistical models, including Tweedie GLM, Negative Binomial, and Hurdle models, are combined with Monte Carlo simulations to generate potential projections through 2030.
  • Interactive Visualization: All results are presented through a web interface where users can explore maps, compare harmonized and unharmonized data, examine protected areas, and analyze historical trends and future projections.

What benefits does it have?

  • Environmental: Improves the reliability of wildfire monitoring, helps identify areas with recurring fire activity, and supports the analysis of threats to ecosystems and protected natural areas.
  • Social: Provides environmental authorities, local communities, and emergency organizations with more consistent information to understand wildfire patterns and improve prevention and response planning.
  • Scientific and Technological: Addresses inconsistencies between satellite sensors through spatial harmonization and statistical calibration, creating a more reliable historical dataset for environmental research and decision-making.
  • Practical: Centralizes historical data, interactive maps, statistical analysis, and future projections in a single platform, making complex satellite information easier to explore and interpret.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, PIXFire aims to provide a reliable historical analysis of wildfire activity in Bolivia, demonstrating how harmonizing data from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors can prevent misleading interpretations caused by differences in their spatial resolutions.

In the long term, the project seeks to expand its coverage to other countries and eventually develop a global wildfire analysis platform. Its vision is to help environmental organizations and authorities anticipate fire risks, improve prevention strategies, protect vulnerable communities, and preserve ecosystems through more reliable data and predictive analysis.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3.
  • Data Processing and Analysis: Python, Pandas, NumPy, statistical modeling, and geospatial data processing.
  • Statistical Models: Tweedie Generalized Linear Models (GLM), Negative Binomial models, Hurdle models, and Monte Carlo simulations.
  • Frontend and Visualization: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet, and interactive data visualization components.
  • Satellite Data Sources: NASA FIRMS, MODIS sensor aboard Aqua, and VIIRS sensor aboard Suomi-NPP.
  • Geospatial Data: Spatial grids, geographic coordinates, and protected area datasets.
  • Development Tools: Python scripts and reproducible data processing pipelines.
  • Data Visualization: Interactive maps, monthly summaries, heat calendars, seasonal charts, and historical trend comparisons.

Artificial Intelligence for Data Analysis and Statistical Modeling

PIXFire incorporates statistical modeling techniques and computational simulations to analyze historical wildfire behavior and generate potential future scenarios. These methods help identify trends, seasonal patterns, and variations in fire activity using previously harmonized satellite data.

  • Tweedie GLM Model: Used to model fire activity and analyze data characterized by numerous zero values and positive observations.
  • Negative Binomial Model: Helps analyze the variability and dispersion of fire activity records, accounting for potential differences across periods and regions.
  • Hurdle Model: Distinguishes between the occurrence of fire activity and its recorded intensity, allowing different behavioral patterns to be analyzed.
  • Monte Carlo Simulations: Used to generate multiple potential scenarios based on statistical models and calculate projection intervals, such as P10–P90, for the 2027–2030 period.
  • Trend and Seasonality Analysis: Examines historical patterns and temporal variations to understand wildfire behavior and support future projections.

Combining these methods transforms harmonized historical records into analytical information and projections that can contribute to wildfire monitoring, planning, and prevention-related decision-making.

Artificial Intelligence as Support for Project Development

During the development of PIXFire, several artificial intelligence tools were used as technological assistants to optimize code, support data processing, and facilitate the preparation of project documentation.

  • OpenCode: Used for source code review, debugging, and optimization, helping identify errors and improve code structure and functionality.
  • Gemini Argon: Used to support the review and processing of code related to statistical modeling and predictive analysis, contributing to the development and refinement of the project's analytical components.
  • Claude: Used as a programming assistant for code review, development tasks, and technical problem-solving.
  • ChatGPT: Used primarily for translation and content writing, as well as improving the clarity and organization of project documentation.

These tools helped optimize the development process, facilitate technical tasks, and improve the preparation of PIXFire's content. Their use complemented the programming, review, and integration work carried out by the team.
